design_detail: Scoping review (Grant and Booth typology; two-stage screening after the Cochrane handbook; PRISMA flow diagram) of primary studies with data on fentanyl test strips (FTS) as a harm-reduction tool, registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) on 6 March 2023. A librarian searched PubMed, Ovid Embase and Web of Science Core Collection on 7 March 2023, English only; 91 articles were included (data collection completed 2016–2022 where reported; 90 of 91 from North America) and sorted into six evidence domains: test accuracy and reliability, acceptability, feasibility of use by the community, feasibility as a public-health intervention, behaviour change after results, and overdose-related outcomes. No appraisal of the included studies and no pooling. Filed as systematic-review because the schema has no scoping-review design, and read with AMSTAR 2 as the batch instructions require; the items a scoping review does not attempt are named in the risk-of-bias reasoning. Read from the PubMed Central author manuscript (19 PDF pages without journal pagination; ‘AM p.’ gives the PDF page) with its supplementary material, read on 27 October 2026: Appendix 1, the complete reference list (95 entries; the manuscript prints 1–50), and Supplemental Tables 1–3 (per-study figures behind the ranges for use, satisfaction and behaviour change).
can_establish: Which kinds of primary studies of fentanyl test strips for harm reduction existed by March 2023 (mostly qualitative and North American, none randomized), which questions they addressed, and the ranges of accuracy, willingness, use, satisfaction and self-reported behaviour change they reported, as the review relays them.
cannot_establish: How accurate fentanyl test strips are when people test at home, whether testing changes what people do, or whether it prevents overdose: the included studies were not appraised, the figures are second-hand ranges from uncontrolled and largely self-reported studies (some about hypothetical results), only two studies reported overdose outcomes, and the supplementary tables behind its ranges mix shares of people with shares of visits, survey answers and instances, and measure earlier use of strips rather than uptake when strips were offered.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). PubMed, Ovid Embase and Web of Science Core Collection were searched on 7 March 2023 by a librarian, with the search terms posted on OSF (not read); no grey-literature, registry, reference-list or expert searches are reported (Methods › Data sources and searches, AM p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: articles with primary data on FTS as a harm-reduction tool (accuracy and reliability, acceptability, feasibility of use by the community, feasibility within public-health interventions, behaviour change after results, overdose-related outcomes), any country and any design, English only; the criteria were kept broad because of the low volume of articles (Methods › Study selection, 2nd paragraph, AM p. 3). Excluded at full text: 50 articles without original data on FTS (Figure 1, AM p. 13). No publication-date limit is stated.
sample.demographics: Not reported per study, except for the 14 studies in Supplemental Table 1 (setting and, for 13 of them, the share of White participants, from 0% to 91.7%). Included articles: United States 58 (64%), Canada 29 (32%), Mexico 3 (3%), Australia 1 (1%); opioids only 13 (14%), opioids and other drugs 69 (76%), non-opioid drugs only 3 (3%); 39 (43%) mainly about FTS; 8,929 participants in all, median 44 per study (Results, 1st paragraph, AM p. 3; Table 1, AM p. 16).
sample.selection_effects: English only, three databases and no grey literature; 90 of 91 studies come from North America, so markets where fentanyl is still rare are almost absent. Recruitment settings are not summarised; the programmes in Table 3 reached people through syringe services, emergency departments, police, a university, hospital addiction care, a contingency-management programme and a vending machine, so people outside services are under-represented. Almost half the studies are qualitative, and acceptability and behaviour-change figures rest on self-report, some about hypothetical results. The rows of Table 1 do not add to 91 (years 83, designs 84, drug types 85; editors' sums), so part of the included set is not characterised.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. In the included studies, FTS were used for drug checking before use, or after use on urine or paraphernalia, and were handed out through syringe services programmes, emergency departments, police departments, pharmacy students, hospital addiction care, a contingency-management programme and a vending machine (Table 3, AM p. 18), usually beside other harm-reduction tools; 52 of 91 articles (57%, editors' calculation) were not mainly about FTS.
exposure.polysubstance: Studies are classed by drug type (Table 1). The review relays FTS detecting fentanyl in heroin, counterfeit pills, cocaine, crystal methamphetamine, xylazine-containing samples, alprazolam and psychedelics, and false positives at high concentrations of several non-opioid drugs (Results › FTS accuracy and reliability, 2nd paragraph, AM p. 3–4). Results are not separated by drug type, apart from statements about people whose drug of choice is not an opioid.

comparison.controls: Not applicable at review level. No included study was randomized; the two studies of behaviour change around FTS distribution (Krieger et al., 2018; Park et al., 2020, by Appendix 1) compared people with positive results against people who did not use FTS or who had negative results, and the two overdose studies had no control group (Results › Behavior Change from FTS Results, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs, AM p. 6; Overdose related outcomes after FTS use, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs, AM p. 7).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a review. The review notes that people who use drugs often practise safer behaviours whether or not they use FTS (Behavior Change from FTS Results, 1st paragraph, AM p. 6), which confounds any comparison of people who test with people who do not.

outcomes.instruments: Narrative mapping by evidence domain: per-study values, ranges and medians relayed from the included studies (willingness, use, interpretation difficulty, post-consumption testing, satisfaction, self-reported positive behaviour change, overdose-related odds ratios), the figures for use, satisfaction and behaviour change from Supplemental Tables 1–3 (read 27 October 2026: Table 1, reported prior use of strips in 14 studies; Table 2, satisfaction in eight rows from seven studies; Table 3, any positive behaviour change at eight locations in seven studies); counts of studies by behaviour in Table 4.
outcomes.validity_norms: The instruments and designs of the included studies are not appraised. ‘Positive behavior change’ is the review's own grouping (not using the drug, using less, going slower, tester shots, using with others, naloxone at hand), and Table 4 counts actual and hypothetical reports side by side. The supplementary tables relabel their sources' measures: Supplemental Table 1's ‘approximate uptake rate’ is each sample's reported prior use of strips (one row a share of visits), and Supplemental Table 3, headed as a percent of participants, includes a share of changes after each positive result (Arendt) and a share of survey answers (Klaire et al.).
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit was operationalised as self-reported positive behaviour change after a result (usually a positive one) and, in two studies, overdose-related outcomes: overdose and naloxone administration at an overdose prevention site, and county overdose deaths and emergency visits after a vending machine was installed.

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled. As relayed (second-hand): sensitivity about 96.3–98% and specificity 89.2–89.4% for fentanyl in drug checking (two studies); willingness to use FTS 43–85% (five studies); documented FTS use 1–80% (median 19%; Supplemental Table 1 gives reported prior use in 13 studies and visits with a check in one, 1% to 81%); difficulty interpreting results 3% to almost 34%; post-consumption testing 13–58%; 49–96% found FTS useful and would use them again (Supplemental Table 2: five percentages from four studies); any self-reported positive behaviour change median 55% (range 23–75%; seven studies, eight locations; Supplemental Table 3, whose 74.9% is a share of instances); in one overdose prevention site study (Karamouzian et al., 2018, ref. 69), odds ratios of 9.36 for intending to reduce the dose after a positive pre-consumption test, and 0.41 for overdose and 0.38 for naloxone administration with reduction intention whatever the result (no intervals printed in the review).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Registered on OSF on 6 March 2023, the day before the search; the search terms and extraction template are said to be posted there (Methods, AM p. 2–3). The registration was not read; no deviations are reported.
analysis.selective_reporting: Per-study values for use, satisfaction and behaviour change are only in Supplemental Tables 1–3, and references 51–95 only in Appendix 1 (all read 27 October 2026). Appendix 1 identifies the figures cited to references above 50: the overdose odds ratios (ref. 69) are Karamouzian et al. (2018), the Rhode Island cohort (ref. 70) is Krieger et al. (2018) and the five-fold higher positivity at home (ref. 66) is Klaire et al. (2022), all three read for this project (sc_karamouzian_2018, sc_krieger_2018, sc_klaire_2022); Table 3's Arendt 2022 (ref. 81) is dated 2023 in Appendix 1, and Park 2020 (ref. 80) is listed again as ref. 93. The supplementary tables give no intervals and no denominators for satisfaction or behaviour change, and the text's ranges do not say that one row of the uptake table counts visits and one value of the behaviour-change table counts instances.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Ninety-one heterogeneous articles (some of them from the same study), 43% qualitative and none randomized, map the field: validation studies relay high sensitivity (about 96–98%) and lower specificity (about 89%) for fentanyl; willingness, use and satisfaction vary widely (use 1–80%, median 19%, which Supplemental Table 1 shows to be mostly earlier use reported by study samples, one row counting visits, not uptake measured after strips were offered); behaviour change is self-reported, partly hypothetical and without comparison groups; two weak studies report overdose-related outcomes. The review's own text describes home testing as error-prone (positive results five times more frequent at home than at a drug-checking programme, in Klaire et al., 2022, where the ratio holds for crystal methamphetamine only; interpretation difficulty up to almost 34%).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that “Robust evidence exists supporting the sensitivity and specificity of FTS”, together with their acceptability and feasibility (AM p. 1), and the Conclusion that FTS are highly sensitive and specific at the point of care (AM p. 9). No accuracy study was appraised, the cited specificity is about 89%, and the body reports reading errors and low uptake, so ‘robust’ and ‘feasible’ go beyond what is shown, at least for testing by people at home. The Discussion calls positive behaviour change after a positive result widely documented (AM p. 8), and the Results infer a likely net increase among people concerned about fentanyl (AM p. 7), from self-reports without comparison groups. The conclusion that evidence for overdose prevention is limited matches the results. The supplement adds to the gap: the text sets acceptability against ‘rates of utilization’ (median 19%), but Supplemental Table 1 gives earlier use in other samples, one row counting visits; and the median of 55% reporting positive change is called a share of participants, while Supplemental Table 3 includes a share of instances (74.9%) and a share of survey answers (25.6%).

timeline.event: Earliest completion year of data collection among the included studies (one study); 16 completed in 2017, 20 in 2019 and 19 in 2021 (Table 1).

Rhode Island pilot of strips for young adults (Krieger et al.): in the review as a willingness paper listed twice (refs 28 and 65, same DOI), its conference abstract (ref. 29), the follow-up paper on use and behaviour change (ref. 70, Krieger et al., 2018, read for this project) and, in Table 3, a qualitative paper by the same team (Goldman et al., 2019, ref. 64); the follow-up paper says the willingness paper reports baseline results from the same pilot (sc_krieger_2018, AM p. 8).

Karamouzian et al.: the drug checking service of a Vancouver supervised injection facility (ref. 69), the source of the review's overdose odds ratios and of the 1% (1,411 of 134,176 visits) in Supplemental Table 1; read for this project.

Peiper et al.: a syringe services programme in the Southeastern United States (ref. 38), in Supplemental Table 1 (prior use 81%, 101 of 125) and Supplemental Table 3 (43% positive behaviour change, located there in Southeast Illinois); also inside Maghsoudi et al. (2022); not read.

Green et al.: limits of detection, sensitivity and specificity of three drug-checking devices on street samples (ref. 15), cited by the review among the sources for accuracy after dilution and the 0.100 mcg/mL detection limit.
Lockwood et al.: false positives on FTS from high concentrations of illicit stimulants and cutting agents (ref. 14); read for this project (sc_lockwood_2021).

Park et al. validation of a lateral flow immunoassay for fentanyl in drug samples (ref. 16) and the Arendt vending-machine evaluation (ref. 81; dated 2022 in Table 3, 2023 in Appendix 1); cited; not read. Klaire et al. (2022), read for this batch, is ref. 66 and is listed again as ref. 92 (Appendix 1): the review's five-fold higher positivity at home, its six participants (1.8%) with riskier behaviour, its 25.6% in Supplemental Table 3 and its 95% in Supplemental Table 2 all come from this study.
OSF registration on 6 March and search on 7 March.
This scoping review published (Journal of Addiction Medicine 18(4):373–380; read as the author manuscript).

Erickson et al. (2026), read for this batch and later than the search: in a rural cohort of people who inject drugs, past-30-day FTS use was lower at 12 months than at baseline, and witnessing an overdose was associated with use.

replication.where_it_stands: A map of the FTS literature to March 2023, not a finding to be replicated. Its accuracy figures should be taken from appraised primary studies (in this project, card sc_green_2020 for one laboratory study). Neither of the related papers read for this batch (Klaire et al., 2022; Erickson et al., 2026) measures overdose, so the review's central gap, the lack of comparative evidence that FTS prevent overdose, still stands in what has been read. Its figures overlap with primary studies that this project's claims cite directly: Krieger et al. (2018), Karamouzian et al. (2018), Klaire et al. (2022), Green et al. (2020), Lockwood et al. (2021) and Bergh et al. (2021) are among its references (Appendix 1), so figures from them are counted once.

funding.funder: Primary funding: NIDA R25DA033211, NIH UL 1TR001445 and HRSA T25HP37605 (Acknowledgments, AM p. 9).
funding.declared_conflicts: Dr. Lee receives in-kind study drugs for an NIH-sponsored clinical trial from Alkermes and Indivior and is a science advisor for Oar Health; no other conflicts are declared (Declarations of Competing Interests, AM p. 1).
funding.affiliations_note: Four authors from NYU Grossman School of Medicine, the first author also from the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, including a librarian (F.L.) who ran the search. The declared interests are in-kind study drugs and an advisory role; none is described as related to test strips. A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A registered systematic review that appraises FTS accuracy studies with QUADAS-2 and keeps laboratory testing apart from testing by people at home, together with comparative studies of FTS distribution (cluster-randomized, or cohorts with concurrent comparison groups) that measure enacted behaviour and overdose.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people who use drugs), intervention (FTS) and outcome domains are named, but there is no comparator; a scoping question does not attempt one.

Registered on OSF on 6 March 2023, the day before the search, with the search terms and extraction template said to be posted there; the registration was not read and no deviations are discussed. No risk-of-bias assessment was done, which AMSTAR 2 expects the protocol to plan; judged partial yes on the registration, as for other registered reviews in this project whose registration was not read.
All designs with primary data were included, explained by the low volume of articles (Methods › Study selection, 2nd paragraph).

Three databases searched by a librarian with the terms on OSF; but English only without justification (named only as a limitation), no grey literature, registries, reference lists or experts, and the stated reliance on peer-reviewed published reports sits beside cited preprints and a conference abstract.
Two reviewers screened titles, abstracts and full texts and resolved discrepancies by consensus (Methods › Study selection, 1st paragraph).
A standardized template is described, but not who extracted or whether a second reviewer checked; papers were reread during writing.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Figure 1 gives one reason and a count (50 full texts without original FTS data); the supplementary material, read on 27 October 2026, is a reference list (Appendix 1) and three tables of results (Supplemental Tables 1–3), with no list of excluded studies.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The 91 studies are described only in aggregate (Table 1); per-study detail is limited to 13 programmes in Table 3 and to the 14, 7 and 7 studies in Supplemental Tables 1–3 (setting, year, a population note and the figure used), with no study-level description of population, intervention, comparator, outcomes and design for the included studies (supplement read 27 October 2026).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No appraisal of any included study; a scoping review does not attempt one.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not among the extracted fields (country, years, design, role of FTS, drug types, evidence domain) and not reported.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Without appraisal, the abstract calls the accuracy evidence robust and the Discussion calls behaviour change widely documented, although the evidence is unappraised, largely self-reported and uncontrolled; the limits of the two overdose studies are noted.

Wide ranges (use 1–80%, willingness 43–85%, behaviour change 23–75%) are reported without investigating their sources; differences between people who use opioids and people who use other drugs, and fentanyl saturation of the market, are proposed but not examined.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and competing interests are declared (AM p. 1; 9).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Items 7 and 8, provisional until the supplement was read, are judged no since 27 October 2026: the supplementary files hold a reference list and three tables of results, with no list of excluded studies and no study-level description. Four critical items are not met (4, search; 7, excluded studies; 9, appraisal; 13, use of appraisal in interpretation) and a fifth (2) only in part, so confidence is critically low. A scoping review maps evidence and does not attempt items 9, 12 and 13 (appraisal and its use), 11 and 15 (meta-analysis and publication bias) or a comparator under item 1; AMSTAR 2 is applied as written, so the rating says how far the review's summary statements can be trusted as appraised evidence, not how good the map is. Citable for: the make-up of the FTS literature to March 2023 (91 articles, none randomized, two with overdose outcomes), the ranges it relays (labelled second-hand, with what its supplementary tables actually measure), and its conclusion that evidence that FTS prevent overdose is limited. Not citable for: the accuracy of FTS (use appraised primary studies), uptake when strips are offered (its use table is mostly earlier use), the size of behaviour change after testing, or any effect on overdose.

key_findings.finding: Scoping review registered on OSF on 6 March 2023; PubMed, Ovid Embase and Web of Science Core Collection searched by a librarian on 7 March 2023; English only; titles, abstracts and full texts screened by two reviewers with consensus; data extracted with a standardized template (country, years of data collection, design, role of FTS, drug types, evidence domain); no appraisal of the included studies.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Methods; Methods › Data sources and searches; Study selection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Extraction and topics

key_findings.finding: Flow: 567 records imported, 247 duplicates removed, 320 screened, 179 excluded as irrelevant, 141 full texts assessed, 50 excluded for lacking original data on FTS, 91 included.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 (flow diagram, read from the rendered image)

key_findings.finding: Included studies (Table 1): no randomized trial; 1 non-randomized experimental study, 8 cohort, 3 cross-sectional, 39 qualitative (43%; interviews 34, surveys 12), 1 case series, 14 diagnostic test accuracy, 5 quality improvement, 13 mixed methods or other; United States 58 (64%), Canada 29 (32%), Mexico 3, Australia 1; 39 (43%) mainly about FTS; opioids only 13, opioids and other drugs 69 (76%), non-opioid drugs only 3; 8,929 participants in all, median 44 per study.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: The design rows add to 84, the year rows to 83 and the drug-type rows to 85 of 91 (editors' sums); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Evidence domains (Table 2; an article can count in several): test accuracy and reliability 16, acceptability to the community 40, feasibility of use by the community 41, feasibility as a public-health intervention 17, behaviour change based on results 37, overdose-related outcomes 2.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: The text calls the behaviour-change share nearly 1 in 3; 37 of 91 is 40.7% (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Accuracy, as relayed: in drug checking, FTS sensitivity about 96.3–98% and specificity 89.2–89.4% for fentanyl (refs. 16, 17); accuracy is described as depending on dilution, with a cited detection limit of 0.100 mcg/mL (refs. 7, 14, 15). FTS detected fentanyl in heroin (‘China white’ and ‘black tar’), counterfeit pills and non-opioid drugs (xylazine-containing samples, alprazolam, cocaine, counterfeit Adderall, crystal methamphetamine, psychedelics).
key_findings.locator: Results › FTS accuracy and reliability, 1st paragraph (AM p. 3) for sensitivity, specificity, dilution and detection limit; 2nd paragraph (begins AM p. 3, continues on AM p. 4) for the drugs in which strips detected fentanyl

key_findings.finding: Limits, as relayed: false positives at high concentrations of cocaine, gabapentin, alprazolam, buprenorphine-naloxone, methamphetamine, MDMA and diphenhydramine (refs. 14, 16), which the review says dilution prevents; acetyl fentanyl and furanylfentanyl test positive, while carfentanil, norcarfentanil and norfentanyl test negative (refs. 15, 16, 25, 26). FTS give no information on xylazine, synthetic cannabinoids, phenacetin, levamisole or etizolam, nor on the amount of fentanyl.
key_findings.locator: Results › FTS accuracy and reliability, 2nd paragraph (begins AM p. 3; these sentences on AM p. 4); Acceptability of FTS use by community › Limitations of FTS in an evolving drug supply, 3rd paragraph (AM p. 4); Discussion, 1st paragraph (AM p. 8)
key_findings.note: The false-positive list cites refs 14 (Lockwood et al., 2021) and 16 (Park et al., 2022). Lockwood et al. found seized cocaine and alprazolam, gabapentin and buprenorphine-naloxone products negative at every concentration tested, up to 20 mg/mL (sc_lockwood_2021), so for those four drugs the list can rest at most on Park et al., which was not read; that dilution prevents these false positives is stated, not tested in the review.

key_findings.finding: Acceptability and use: willingness to use FTS 43–85% (five studies, refs. 33–37); documented use 1–80% (median 19%; Supplemental Table 1, which gives reported prior use of strips in 13 studies and visits with a check in one, from 1% to 81%); 49–96% found FTS useful and wanted to use them again (Supplemental Table 2: five percentages from four studies, all stated intentions to use strips again). Use of drug checking services was more likely among people who had witnessed an overdose in the past 6 months, suspected fentanyl exposure, injected in public, did sex work or had had a non-fatal overdose (one study, ref. 63, which Appendix 1 identifies as Beaulieu et al., 2020, on drug checking services in Vancouver).
key_findings.locator: Results › Acceptability of FTS use by community, 1st paragraph; Feasibility of FTS Use, 1st paragraph; Feasibility of FTS Use › Overall satisfaction with use, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Ease of use: FTS are often called easy but can be error prone; positive results were five times more frequent at home than at a drug-checking programme (ref. 66, Klaire et al., 2022); difficulty interpreting results ranged from 3% to almost 34% (refs. 38, 39, 52: Peiper et al., 2019, Tilhou et al., 2022, and Park et al., 2021, all at US syringe services programmes); misbeliefs included that line intensity shows fentanyl purity and that a negative result indicates xylazine; whether training helps is unclear.
key_findings.locator: Results › Feasibility of FTS Use › Ease of use, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Post-consumption testing (urine or paraphernalia) by 13–58% of participants in the studies cited (refs. 38, 47, 58, 66, 68, 69). Barriers are led by the illegality of drugs and paraphernalia and, in some places, of FTS themselves (Figure 2); facilitators include a safe or private place to test, recommendation by staff, delivery, more strips at once, packaging and instructions (Figure 3).
key_findings.locator: Results › Feasibility of FTS Use › Timing of FTS Use with relation to drug use, 1st paragraph; Barriers and facilitators to use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figures 2–3 (read from the rendered images)
key_findings.note: The text says seven studies but cites six references, none listed twice in Appendix 1: Peiper et al. (2019), Duncan Cance et al. (2023), Betsos et al. (2022), Klaire et al. (2022), Beaulieu et al. (2021) and Karamouzian et al. (2018).

key_findings.finding: Distribution programmes (Table 3) mostly report numbers handed out; few report a net change in FTS use. Examples: 62 of 93 young adults given 10 strips returned 2–4 weeks later having used at least one (Goldman 2019); 57 of 103 female sex workers returned and reported using at least one (Park 2020); 17,000 strips over 7 months, with use of 70% in Baltimore and 77% in Delaware (Park 2021); 16 of 23 emergency department patients offered strips took them home (Lima 2022); police handed out 320 kits in 3 months, with 318 referrals or follow-up services (Olson 2022).
key_findings.locator: Results › Feasibility of FTS distribution as a public health intervention, 1st paragraph; Table 3
key_findings.note: Appendix 1: Goldman 2019 (ref. 64) is a qualitative paper by the Rhode Island team (Krieger, Yedinak and Marshall among its authors), and its row gives the counts of that pilot (Krieger et al., 2018: 62 of 81 analysed used a strip; 93 enrolled); Park 2020 is ref. 80 (listed again as 93), Park 2021 ref. 52, Lima 2022 ref. 89 and Olson 2022 ref. 73.

key_findings.finding: Behaviour change around distribution, two studies: young adults who inject drugs in Rhode Island (prospective cohort, ref. 70), 68% of those with a positive result reported positive behaviour change against 32% of those who did not use FTS; female sex workers in Baltimore (n = 103, ref. 80), 67% after a positive result against 10% after a negative one, and a significant decrease in self-reported use of illicit opioids and benzodiazepines among those who used at least one strip (no figures given).
key_findings.locator: Results › Behavior Change from FTS Results, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Introduced as studies of behaviour before and after counselling and distribution, but the figures compare groups (positive result against no use or a negative result), with no control group. Appendix 1: ref. 70 is Krieger et al. (2018), the Rhode Island pilot read for this project (sc_krieger_2018), where 68% is 21 of 31 with a positive result and 32% is 6 of 19 who used no strip, on a composite of changes from baseline (Krieger Table 3); the pilot recruited young adults who injected or used heroin, cocaine or street-bought pills, so ‘who inject drugs’ does not describe all of them. Ref. 80 is Park et al. (2020), listed again as ref. 93.

key_findings.finding: In seven studies that did not introduce FTS as an intervention, a median 55% (range 23–75%) of participants across eight locations reported any positive behaviour change (Supplemental Table 3: 23% to 74.9%, the top value a share of instances). The commonest changes were using smaller amounts (17 studies in Table 4: 14 actual, 3 hypothetical), not using the drug (14), going slower (10) and tester shots (8). Some people used as usual after a positive result because of withdrawal, existing harm-reduction practice, tolerance, scepticism about the result or a preference for fentanyl.
key_findings.locator: Results › Behavior Change from FTS Results, 4th and 5th paragraphs; Table 4
key_findings.note: Confirmed by Supplemental Table 3 (read 27 October 2026), as the earlier readers suspected: its footnote says Arendt's 74.9% is a percentage of changes after each positive detection among 66 clients, not of people, and Klaire et al.'s 25.6% is a share of 336 survey answers (sc_klaire_2022), so the median mixes people, instances and answers.

key_findings.finding: Riskier responses: participants in two studies said they used or would use more, or faster, after testing (one said a negative result would mean using a little more); in one study six participants (1.8% of the sample) reported riskier behaviour after a positive result (ref. 66). 80% of people using stimulants reported hypothetical positive change (refs. 30, 36, 57), though a positive result might lead some to believe they tolerate fentanyl (ref. 31).
key_findings.locator: Results › Behavior Change from FTS Results, 7th and 8th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Appendix 1: refs 47 and 66 are Duncan Cance et al. (2023, a qualitative study in Austin, Texas) and Klaire et al. (2022), whose six (1.8%) are 6 of 336 answers; refs 30, 36 and 57 (stimulants) are Reed et al. (2022), Kennedy et al. (2018) and Reed et al. (2021, listed again as ref. 72); ref. 31 is McKnight and Des Jarlais (2018).

key_findings.finding: Engagement in care: two studies reported more referrals to other services, with no data on engagement in or retention in addiction treatment (refs. 71, 73).
key_findings.locator: Results › Behavior Change from FTS Results, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: Appendix 1: refs 71 and 73 are Mema et al. (2018, a pilot of fentanyl urine testing in rural British Columbia) and Olson et al. (2022, police and community provision of strips in Massachusetts).

key_findings.finding: Overdose-related outcomes in 2 of 91 studies. At a Vancouver overdose prevention site (ref. 69), drug checking followed 1% of visits and was mostly post-consumption; among pre-consumption tests a positive result was associated with intending to reduce the dose (odds ratio 9.36), and reduction intention, whatever the result, with lower odds of overdose (0.41) and of naloxone administration (0.38); no intervals are printed.
key_findings.locator: Results › Overdose related outcomes after FTS use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Appendix 1: ref. 69 is Karamouzian et al. (2018), read for this project (sc_karamouzian_2018).

key_findings.finding: A vending machine in Hamilton County, Ohio (Arendt 2022, ref. 81), dispensed 10,155 FTS with naloxone and injection supplies in its first year; 105 clients surveyed reported 937 fentanyl detections and 702 instances of discarding the drug or using less; county overdose deaths fell about 10% while Ohio's rose about 5%, with fewer overdose-related emergency visits. The review notes confounding by the naloxone from the same machine and the absence of a control group.
key_findings.locator: Results › Overdose related outcomes after FTS use, 3rd paragraph; Table 3
key_findings.note: Appendix 1 gives ref. 81 as Arendt (2023), Journal of the American Pharmacists Association 63(1):309–316; Table 3 dates it 2022.

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that only limited data suggest FTS decrease overdose rates or deaths; that randomized trials face ethical and logistical challenges, so rigorous comparative cohort studies are needed; and that more comprehensive drug checking (FTIR, GC/MS) is likely more acceptable and feasible than single-substance strips. Named limitations: English only, literature to March 2023, reliance on peer-reviewed published reports.
key_findings.locator: Results › Overdose related outcomes after FTS use, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 5th to 7th paragraphs; Conclusion

key_findings.finding: Discussion: FTS show presence only, not concentration, and are called increasingly anachronistic where fentanyl dominates the supply; Canadian samples had a mean fentanyl concentration of 7–8.9%, with more than 16% above 17.7% (refs. 60, 82). People who do not use opioids are proposed as the ideal target group, alongside public-health messaging to treat all drugs as if they contain fentanyl.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Appendix 1: refs 60 and 82 are Larnder et al. (2022, variability in the unregulated opioid market) and Tobias et al. (2022, a time series of fentanyl concentration in a Canadian setting).

key_findings.finding: Supplemental Table 1 (Baseline Uptake Rate of Fentanyl Test Strips), behind the text's documented use of 1–80% (median 19%), lists 14 studies (data 2016–2021; 10 US and 4 Canadian samples) and turns each one's reported prior use of strips into an approximate uptake rate: Walters et al. (rural Illinois) 21% (just under a quarter of 19), Urmanche et al. (New York City, people preferring fentanyl) 36% (8 of 22), Rhodes et al. (Durham, North Carolina) 16% (4 of 25), Rammohan et al. (Toronto, overdose prevention site) 8% (51 of 604), Oh et al. (San Francisco) 45.4% (208 of 458), Long et al. (Vancouver) 21% (176 of 828), Beaulieu et al. (Vancouver, ref. 68) 13.7% (196 of 1426), Bass et al. (Philadelphia, syringe services) 20% (4 of 20), Tilhou et al. (southern Wisconsin, syringe services) 80% (274 of 341), Stein et al. (Fall River, Massachusetts, inpatient opioid withdrawal management) 1% (3 of 239), Peiper (Southeastern US) 81% (101 of 125), Mistler (New Haven, methadone patients) 17% (18 of 105), Karamouzian (Vancouver) 1% (1411 visits of 134,176) and Allen (Appalachia) 2% (1 of 48).
key_findings.locator: Supplemental Table 1, all 14 rows (columns Reported Prior Use of FTS and Approximate Uptake Rate) and footnote
key_findings.note: The top value is 81% (Peiper), not the text's 80%; the median of the 14 printed rates is 18.5% (editors' calculation; printed 19%); one row counts visits with a check, not people (Karamouzian et al., 2018, read for this project); the Rhode Island pilot is not in the table; Stein et al. (2019) is cited only in the table's footnote and is not in Appendix 1.

key_findings.finding: Supplemental Table 2 (Overall Satisfaction with Experience Using FTS), behind the text's 49–96%: eight rows from seven studies. Five rows give the percentage who would use strips again: Park et al. (ref. 52) Baltimore 2019, 123 participants, 49%, and Delaware 2019, 102, 74%; Sutherland (ref. 91) Sydney, Australia, 2021, 78, 96% if strips were free (98% would recommend them to peers); Krieger (ref. 29) Rhode Island 2017, 93, 95% (71% thought friends would be interested); Klaire (ref. 92) Vancouver 2019, 218, 95%. The other three give median ratings of 8.5 and 8.4 out of 10 for ease and clarity (Swartz, ref. 42, Chicago, 12), a statement that most had positive experiences (Walters et al., ref. 37, rural Illinois, 23) and mixed views (Betsos, ref. 58, Vancouver, 26).
key_findings.locator: Supplemental Table 2, all eight rows
key_findings.note: Two of the five percentages are studies read for this project, labelled with the enrolled or returning sample: Krieger's 95% is 77 of 81 analysed in the pilot (sc_krieger_2018), and Klaire's 95% is 322 of 336 answers (95.8%) from 218 people at ten British Columbia sites (sc_klaire_2022). The top value, 96%, comes from ref. 91, a one-page item in a Drug and Alcohol Review supplement (by its form a conference abstract).

key_findings.finding: Supplemental Table 3 (Percent of Participants Reporting a Positive Behavior Change from FTS Results), behind the text's median of 55% (range 23–75%) in seven studies at eight locations: Park et al. (ref. 52) Baltimore 23% and Delaware 69%; Peiper et al. (ref. 38) 43%; Oh et al. (ref. 55, San Francisco) 56.6%; Klaire et al. (ref. 66) 25.6%; Goodman-Meza (ref. 19, northern Mexico) 53.3%; Arendt et al. (ref. 81, Cincinnati, Ohio) 74.9%, which a footnote calls a percentage of changes after each positive fentanyl detection among 66 clients; Mema et al. (ref. 71) 66.7%.
key_findings.locator: Supplemental Table 3, all eight rows and footnote
key_findings.note: Median of the eight values 54.95% (editors' calculation). The top value counts instances (702 of 937 detections, AM p. 7), not people, and Klaire et al.'s 25.6% is their 86 of 336 answers to a standard question (sc_klaire_2022). The table places Peiper et al. in Southeast Illinois (Supplemental Table 1 and the title of ref. 38: the Southeastern United States) and Mema et al. in Vancouver (title of ref. 71: rural British Columbia).

key_findings.finding: Appendix 1 (Complete Reference List, 95 entries) identifies the references above 50 that carry key figures: 52 Park et al. (2021, two Mid-Atlantic syringe services programmes); 63 Beaulieu et al. (2020, witnessing an overdose and use of drug checking services in Vancouver); 64 Goldman et al. (2019, a qualitative study whose authors include Krieger, Yedinak and Marshall of the Rhode Island pilot); 66 Klaire et al. (2022, take-home drug checking in British Columbia); 69 Karamouzian et al. (2018, the drug checking service of a Vancouver supervised injection facility); 70 Krieger et al. (2018, use of strips among young adults, International Journal of Drug Policy); 71 Mema et al. (2018, fentanyl urine testing in rural British Columbia); 80 Park et al. (2020, female sex workers in Baltimore); 81 Arendt (2023, an automated dispensing machine). Four entries are listed twice with the same DOI (28 and 65, Krieger et al.'s 2018 willingness paper; 57 and 72, Reed et al., 2021; 66 and 92; 80 and 93), and 29 is a conference abstract of 28.
key_findings.note: Studies read for this project that are among the review's references: Bergh et al. (ref. 7), Lockwood et al. (14), Green et al. (15), Klaire et al. (66 and 92), Karamouzian et al. (69) and Krieger et al. (70); DOIs match the project's reference records. Editors' count: nine entries are not studies (web pages, press releases, a commentary and methods references: 1, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13) and four are repeats, so the list names at most 82 distinct articles, 85 with the three studies cited only in footnotes (Stein et al., 2019, under Supplemental Table 1; two under Figure 3), fewer than the 91 included.

reporting_issues.issue: The rows of Table 1 do not add to 91 and have no ‘not reported’ row: years of data collection add to 83, designs to 84 and drug types to 85 (editors' sums). Within qualitative research (39), interviews (34) and surveys (12) add to 46, and surveys are classed as qualitative research.
reporting_issues.consequence: The design profile cannot be reconstructed exactly; ‘almost half qualitative’ depends on counting surveys as qualitative.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Results say all included studies were conducted after 2016; Table 1 lists one study whose data collection was completed in 2016.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the earliest data may date from 2016.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say nearly 1 in 3 articles reported the effect of FTS results on behaviour; Table 2 gives 37 of 91 (40.7%, editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite the count in Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: Counts of studies in the text do not match their citations: ‘seven studies’ on post-consumption testing cite six references (38, 47, 58, 66, 68, 69); ‘two studies’ preferring pre-consumption testing cite three (28, 38, 70), but 28 and 70 are papers from the same Rhode Island pilot (Appendix 1; Krieger et al., AM p. 8), so that count holds; the text names two studies of using more or faster, Table 4 three (66 and 47 actual, 94 hypothetical).
reporting_issues.consequence: Study counts in the text cannot always be relied on; cite the ranges as relayed, not the number of studies.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 counts reference 95 in both the actual and the hypothetical column for going slower, using with another person and not using the drug, so those totals (10, 7, 14) exceed the distinct references (9, 6, 13; editors' count).
reporting_issues.consequence: The totals count mentions, not studies; each overstates by one.

reporting_issues.issue: The manuscript prints only references 1–50 and puts the full list in Appendix 1; key figures cite references above 50 (for example 63, 66, 69, 70, 80, 81). Appendix 1 (read 27 October 2026) identifies them: 63 Beaulieu et al. (2020), 66 Klaire et al. (2022), 69 Karamouzian et al. (2018), 70 Krieger et al. (2018), 80 Park et al. (2020), 81 Arendt (2023).
reporting_issues.consequence: Resolved by the appendix: three of these primary studies (refs 66, 69 and 70) were read for this project and are cited directly in its claims, so the review's figures from them are counted once with the primary studies.

reporting_issues.issue: References 28 and 29, cited together, are a 2018 journal article and a 2018 conference abstract with the same title and first author. Appendix 1 also lists the journal article a second time (ref. 65, same DOI), ref. 70 is the follow-up paper of the same Rhode Island pilot, whose authors say the willingness paper reports its baseline (Krieger et al., AM p. 8), and Table 3's Goldman 2019 row (ref. 64) is a qualitative paper by the same team with the pilot's counts.
reporting_issues.consequence: One pilot appears under five reference numbers; if several are among the 91 included articles, the count of articles overstates the number of studies, and figures from them must be counted once.

reporting_issues.issue: The limitations name reliance on peer-reviewed published reports, but the Results cite a medRxiv preprint (ref. 20), a Research Square preprint (ref. 42) and a conference abstract (ref. 29), and Supplemental Table 2 takes its top value (96%) from a one-page item in a Drug and Alcohol Review supplement (ref. 91, by its form a conference abstract) and a satisfaction rating from the Research Square preprint (ref. 42).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either inclusion was broader than stated or the limitation is misstated; preprint data are relayed as findings.

reporting_issues.issue: The two studies said to investigate behaviour change before and after FTS counselling and distribution are reported as comparisons between groups (68% after a positive result against 32% among people who did not use FTS; 67% after a positive against 10% after a negative result); only the Baltimore decrease in self-reported drug use is a before–after change, given without figures or a comparison group. Appendix 1 identifies the first study as Krieger et al. (2018, ref. 70), where 68% is 21 of 31 with a positive result and 32% is 6 of 19 who used no strip (Krieger Table 3), and the second as Park et al. (2020, ref. 80).
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither study can show that FTS caused the behaviour change; the comparisons are confounded by who chooses to test.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4's column of actual behaviour change after a result includes ref. 69 (Karamouzian et al., 2018: the Vancouver supervised injection site, where staff recorded stated intentions, as the review itself describes it on AM p. 7) and Klaire et al. (2022), as ref. 66 in three rows and as ref. 92 in two, whose answers were to standard questions and could be hypothetical (Appendix 1; sc_klaire_2022). No row counts one study twice through the repeated entries.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 'actual' counts overstate how much enacted behaviour was observed; cite Table 4 as counts of studies reporting each change, not as observed behaviour.

reporting_issues.issue: The review says positive results were five times more frequent at home than at a drug-checking programme (ref. 66, Klaire et al., 2022, by Appendix 1). In that study the ratio was about 5 for crystal methamphetamine (27.6% against 5.2%), about 16 for cocaine (17.2% against 1.1%) and about 1 for opioids (90.0% against 89.1%) (editors' calculation from sc_klaire_2022), and its 'six participants (1.8% of the sample)' were 6 of 336 survey answers from 218 people, as Klaire et al. themselves label them.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 'five times' figure holds for one stimulant only and should not be cited as a general ratio of home to service positivity.

reporting_issues.issue: Supplemental Table 1 is headed as a baseline uptake rate, and the text calls its range rates of utilization, but its rates are the samples' reported prior use of strips, except one row (Karamouzian, 1411 of 134,176 visits), which is a share of visits; the top value is 81% (Peiper, 101 of 125) where the text says 80%, and one study (Stein et al., 2019) is cited only in the table's footnote.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 1–80% (median 19%) is mostly earlier use reported by samples chosen by setting (from inpatients to syringe services clients), not uptake measured after strips were offered, and is set against willingness measured in other studies; it should not be cited as how many people use strips when they are offered.

reporting_issues.issue: Supplemental Table 3 is headed as a percent of participants, but its Arendt value (74.9%) is, by its own footnote, a share of changes after each positive detection, and its Klaire et al. value (25.6%) a share of 336 survey answers from 218 people; its locations for Peiper et al. (Southeast Illinois) and Mema et al. (Vancouver) differ from Supplemental Table 1 and from the titles in Appendix 1 (the Southeastern United States; rural British Columbia).
reporting_issues.consequence: The median of 55% mixes people, instances and answers; cite it as a median of mixed measures, and count Klaire et al.'s value once with the primary study.

reporting_issues.issue: Supplemental Table 2 labels Klaire's 95% as of 218 participants and Krieger's 95% as of 93; the primary studies give 322 of 336 answers (95.8%) and 77 of 81 analysed (95%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the satisfaction range is of stated intentions and two of its five values are studies read for this project.

reporting_issues.issue: Appendix 1 lists four studies twice with the same DOI (28 and 65, 57 and 72, 66 and 92, 80 and 93) and holds nine sources that are not studies; editors' count, it names at most 82 distinct articles, 85 with the three studies cited only in footnotes, fewer than the 91 included articles.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 91 included articles cannot be reconstructed from the references, and the count is of articles, some from the same study, not of independent studies. The repeated entries do not inflate any row of Table 4 (apart from ref. 95, counted in two columns: issue 4).
